title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to evaluate whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only baseline. Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms); the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline safe = 240/240, guarded safe = 240/240. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the single shared generation passed deterministic validation in every task and no validator‑triggered repairs occurred; consequently the paired contrast is degenerate and uninformative about verifier benefit in this run. We report the preregistered design, execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, a mechanistic failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into safe device configurations is a central NetOps challenge. Large language models (LLMs) can generate candidate configuration sequences but text‑level similarity does not guarantee ordering, dependency, or invariant preservation required for safe application. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configs are executed in device images or simulators and deterministically scored—exposes semantic failure modes (ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only tests miss [1].

A common engineering pattern is generate–validate–repair (GVR): (1) an LLM generates an initial candidate; (2) a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants and execution safety; (3) when violations are detected an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate and the verifier rechecks. Prior work reports that GVR‑style designs reduce syntactic and many semantic faults in benchmarked settings, but open empirical questions remain about verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and about experimental designs that reliably expose a causal paired difference between guarded and unguarded pipelines [2][3][4].

This paper reports a fully preregistered paired experiment that measured one precise estimand—the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline)—executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics. We preserve and reference archived execution and analysis artifacts. Our contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded report of a preregistered paired GVR experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) explicit mapping from preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs and exact numerical results; and (3) a mechanistic, artifact‑based failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome and concrete recommendations for future informative designs.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents have been proposed to surface workflow and planning faults rather than only textual fidelity; NetConfArena exemplifies this approach [1]. Research on automatic configuration and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that deterministic validators can enable high repair coverage for certain classes of faults, albeit with limits tied to verifier coverage and repair search strategies [2][4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as important patterns for NetOps automation and safety [3][5]. The engineering evolution of configuration analysis tools (e.g., Batfish) provides precedent for verifier design and incremental verification strategies [6].

Our study differs in three ways: (a) a preregistered paired estimand explicitly mapping to archived analysis artifacts; (b) execution under shared_initial_candidate semantics with deterministic per‑task pairing; and (c) closed‑loop, emulator‑based binary scoring of final configurations against semantic invariants, enabling unambiguous pass/fail outcomes per episode.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate), where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied and safe_apply = 0 otherwise. The analysis plan specified a paired contingency analysis using a permutation/bootstrap estimator (paired bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and an exact two‑sided McNemar test for discordant pairs.

Design and sampling: We used a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each of N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks a single initial LLM generation was produced and reused by both arms; the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. Task composition was 60% in‑distribution (144 tasks), 20% distribution‑shift (48 tasks), and 20% adversarial‑prompt (48 tasks). Tasks were generated deterministically by a registered task generator and contained explicit initial states, required step sequences, and preserved‑field constraints representing realistic maintenance and failover workflows.

Model, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier (validator id reported in the archive). The adapter contract's shared_initial_candidate semantics implies that the only way to create discordant paired outcomes is for the shared initial generation to fail deterministic validation (triggering repair) or for the guarded arm to apply a repair that changes the final configuration relative to the baseline.

Scoring and exclusions: Final outcomes were binary (safe vs unsafe) determined by emulator execution and deterministic invariant checks. Preregistered exclusions included pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (verifier PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) and infra failures after allowed retries; the retry policy allowed up to two infra‑retries per task. The primary analysis excluded items flagged as 'possible false‑safe' per preregistration and provided sensitivity analyses treating such items as unsafe.

Statistical procedures: The primary executor computed the paired contingency table, paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test. Secondary planned metrics included median repair‑iteration count and model‑call budget per task.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed as preregistered. Episodes planned = 480; episodes completed = 480; complete pairs = 240. Exactly one initial generation per task was produced and consumed (model call accounting consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics). No infra failures or preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Baseline safe = 240/240 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0); guarded safe = 240/240 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). The paired contingency counts are n11 (both safe) = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. The paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied across guarded episodes (repair attempt count = 0). Representative validator traces show that validation recorded parsed command counts, touched field counts, difficulty labels, and PASS/FAIL outcomes; in every task the shared initial generation passed deterministic validation and no repair prompt was invoked.

Planned sensitivity channels: The preregistered sensitivity analyses (treat possible false‑safe flags or infra failures as unsafe) were not exercised because no such flags or failures occurred; subgroup analyses by in‑distribution, shift, and adversarial slices are degenerate (all zeros) given identical safe outcomes.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: Under shared_initial_candidate semantics a single LLM generation is produced per task and reused across both arms. The guarded arm can alter the paired outcome only by invoking a validator‑triggered repair that changes the final configuration. In this execution every shared initial generation passed the deterministic validator, so the guarded arm never invoked repair and neither arm produced unsafe applies. Thus the degenerate contingency (no discordant pairs) is a direct consequence of the preregistered generation semantics combined with validator PASS outcomes; this mechanistic account is supported by the recorded model‑call and validation counts.

Design implications and lessons learned: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduces model‑call budget and yields an exact sample‑paired comparison of the same LLM candidate, but it also prevents generator variability between arms and therefore makes the ability to detect verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures. To obtain informative paired contrasts for verifier effectiveness researchers should consider one or more of the following, depending on the estimand of interest: (A) permit independent initial generations per arm so the intervention includes constrained prompting or guard‑aware generation; (B) retain shared pairing but strengthen adversary protocols or inject controlled perturbations to the initial generation to increase opportunities for validation failures; (C) increase repair budget (allow multiple iterative repairs) and instrument repair proposals to analyze repair search behavior. Each option trades model‑call budget, interpretability of causal contrasts, and operational realism differently; experimenters should select the contract matching their causal estimand.

Threats to validity: Internal validity—shared_initial_candidate semantics is an explicit design choice that constrains causal interpretation; it must be considered when defining the estimand. Construct validity—the deterministic validator encodes a finite set of checks and may not cover all semantic fault classes; planned cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes are necessary in other runs to detect false‑safe behavior. External validity—tasks were drawn from a NetConfArena‑style emulation corpus; extrapolation to production multi‑vendor deployments and operator workflows is limited. Conclusion validity—the observed baseline unsafe rate of zero prevents detecting verifier benefit under the executed contract; sample size and adversary strength should be recalibrated in future designs to ensure informative discordant pairs.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration using shared_initial_candidate semantics. Observed outcome: all 240 paired tasks were safe under both arms, producing a paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The degenerate paired result is a mechanistic consequence of the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single shared LLM generation passed deterministic validation for every task, so no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the guarded arm could not create discordant outcomes. This artifact‑grounded result does not imply that deterministic verification is ineffective in general; rather, it highlights how generation semantics, adversary strength, and repair budgets must be chosen to create informative paired contrasts. We provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future GVR evaluations: relax shared pairing when the goal is to evaluate generator‑aware guards, increase adversary or perturbation strength, and expand repair iteration budgets while instrumenting repair proposals. These design choices will increase the probability of generating discordant pairs and thereby allow rigorous estimation of verifier benefit under paired designs.

disclosure_statement: Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline used a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered as study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01 (preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, experiment design, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. Preregistered generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract the paired contrast could only differ if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Immutable master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). A high‑level execution manifest and analysis archive are available in the study bundle; detailed per‑file provenance and raw artifacts are preserved in that archive but are not reprinted here. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected and should be extended in future evaluations.
